Active physical treatment, which includes aerobic and core strengthening exercises, combined with graded activity and problem-solving training, was compared to graded activity with problem-solving training alone. This comparison was part of the WHO guideline for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults. 2. The study by Dalichau (2003) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a high overall risk of bias, with a total of 90 participants. The authors reported greater pain reduction in the exercise group compared to no or no additional treatment, but the effect estimates were unclear. 3. The study by McIlveen (1998) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a high overall risk of bias, with a total of 95 participants. The McGill Pain Questionnaire (1-5 scale) indicated benefits with lower values. 4. The study by Smeets (2008) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a low overall risk of bias, with a total of 119 participants. Participants performed a combination treatment (active physical treatment with aerobic and core strengthening exercises plus graded activity with problem-solving training) compared to graded activity with problem-solving training alone. 5. The study by Sokhanguei (2017) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a high overall risk of bias, with a total of 34 participants. The intervention involved Pilates exercises compared to no or no additional treatment. 6. The study by Kanwal (2021) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a high overall risk of bias, with a total of 24 participants. The intervention involved core strengthening exercises compared to no or no additional treatment. 7. Lang (2021) conducted a study involving aerobic exercise with 174 participants. No harms were reported. 8. Miyamoto (2013) conducted a study involving Pilates exercises with 86 participants. No harms were reported. 9. Rahbar (2018) conducted a study involving core strengthening exercises with 80 participants. No harms were reported. 10. Rotter (2022) conducted a study involving aerobic exercise with 55 participants. No harms were reported. 11. Smeets (2008) reported that 3 participants (5%) in the exercise group experienced increased back pain. This study involved mixed exercises with 119 participants. 12. Weiner (2008) conducted a study on older adults involving mixed exercises with 200 participants. No significant intervention-associated adverse events were reported, although one participant (2%) experienced increased back pain. 13. The study by Raza (2020) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a high overall risk of bias, with a total of 40 participants. The intervention involved stretching or flexibility/mobilizing exercises. 14. The study by Rathi (2013) was excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing data. It was rated as having a high overall risk of bias, with a total of 30 participants. The intervention involved core strengthening exercises, with benefits indicated by lower Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores (0-10 scale). 15. The risk of bias was downgraded twice because most or all trials were rated as having a high overall risk of bias. 16. Inconsistency was not downgraded because the majority of point estimates were similar, with overlapping confidence intervals. However, the I² statistic was 97%, indicating considerable heterogeneity that could not be explained by small subgroups. 17. Indirectness was not downgraded because trials were conducted in both highand low-income countries. 18.
